teaser: Three men, one floor, and a jury that called the subject vulgar.
review_notes:
Setting: usually said to be the Caillebotte family home, rue de Miromesnil, Paris, in the room being prepared as the artist's studio.
Rejected by the Salon jury of 1875; shown at the second Impressionist exhibition, 1876.
Zola's 1876 comment is paraphrased, not quoted.
Bequest figures: about 68 works left to the State, about 40 accepted; The Floor Scrapers entered the national collections in 1894 as a gift of the heirs through Renoir, the executor.
The description of who does which task (plane vs scraper, the left man reaching for a file) is a reading of the image; the tools are small.
Perspective lines are approximate, following the edges of the dark stripes.
Size 102 x 146.5 cm.

lesson.text: When did you last see a painting of people at work? Not a goddess, a general or a bowl of peaches, but somebody doing a job, on their knees, in a city apartment. In Paris in 1875 the honest answer was: almost never. Peasants in fields were acceptable. Workers from the city were not a subject for art.

Gustave Caillebotte was 26 and had just finished his training in the studio of a respected academic painter. His family owned a grand house in a new district of Paris, and a room there was being fitted out for him. Three men came to refinish the oak floor. He watched them, made drawings, and painted this.

lesson.title: Three men
lesson.text: All three are stripped to the waist, kneeling, arms stretched forward.

spots.title: The one apart
spots.text: At left, a man works alone, face in shadow, his mustache just visible. He reaches across the boards toward a small tool lying beside a drift of shavings.

spots.title: The middle man
spots.text: Arms locked straight, both hands on his tool, he pulls it toward himself along a board. His head tilts toward his neighbor.

spots.title: His neighbor
spots.text: Same pose, mirrored. This one turns his head and seems to say something. Two workers chatting through a long afternoon: a tiny, true observation.

lesson.text: The stripes explain the job. The dark bands are old varnished wood that has not been touched yet. The pale areas are bare oak, already scraped. First the men plane down the ridges where boards meet, then they scrape the surface thin layer by thin layer. Curls of wood collect everywhere.

Caillebotte records their trade with a kind of respect: the blades, the hammer for knocking down nails, the bag of tools by the wall. He also records how they get through the day. One object in this room has nothing to do with woodwork.
The men have brought something to drink. Where is it?

spots.title: Wine and a glass
spots.text: On the right, on a marble hearth, a dark bottle and a small glass filled with red. Ordinary wine was part of a laborer's working day in Paris. Caillebotte passes no judgment.

lesson.text: A moralizing painter would have made that bottle a warning. Here it is simply there, like the hammer. This refusal to comment is what bothered people. The picture shows poor men working hard for a rich household, half naked, and offers neither pity nor a lesson.
Caillebotte sent the painting to the Salon, the huge official exhibition that could make a career. The jury of 1875 turned it down. The subject was judged vulgar: workers, bare torsos, a floor.

So he changed sides. In 1876 he hung it with a group of painters who had been mocked two years earlier as “Impressionists”: Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro. It was one of the most discussed pictures in their second show. The novelist Zola admired the nerve but found the precision too clean, almost like a photograph.

Zola had a point. Monet dissolved things in light, while Caillebotte draws every board. What makes the picture modern is somewhere else: the place you are standing. You look steeply down at the floor, as if from a stepladder, and the room tips toward you.
Trace the floorboards and see what they do to the space.

lines.label: A board edge
lines.text: Follow the edge of a dark stripe from the bottom of the canvas. It races away from you, climbing almost the whole height of the picture.

lines.label: Another, leaning in
lines.text: On the right the boards lean the other way. The stripes squeeze together as they go back, like railway tracks, and pull your eye deep into the room.

lines.label: Where the floor ends
lines.text: The wall begins only here. Three quarters of the painting is floor. The horizon is pushed so high that the workers seem to slide toward you.

lesson.text: Over that tilted floor comes the light, straight at you from the balcony window. It turns the wet, scraped wood into a mirror and leaves the men as dark shapes edged with shine along their backs and arms. Their muscles are drawn as carefully as those of a Greek hero in an art school exercise.

Caillebotte did not need to sell. His father had made a fortune supplying cloth and bedding to the French army, and died in 1874, leaving his sons rich. Gustave was trained as a lawyer and later designed and raced his own sailing yachts.

spots.title: The balcony
spots.text: A window with a curling wrought-iron railing, the mark of a smart new Paris building. Outside, pale roofs dissolve in the glare. All the light in the picture enters here.

spots.title: Shavings
spots.text: Thin curls of oak, each painted with one or two twists of the brush. They are scattered all over, telling you where the blades have already passed.

spots.title: The hammer
spots.text: Lying between the two men with its handle toward us, ready for driving down any nail head that would nick a blade.

spots.title: Hands on the tool
spots.text: Both fists grip a block with a blade set in it. The straight arms turn the whole upper body into a lever.

spots.title: Gilded panels
spots.text: White wall paneling with gold moldings. The room is elegant, which makes the bare backs below it even more unexpected.

spots.title: Signature and date
spots.text: “G. Caillebotte 1875”, written large in dark paint on the bare boards, slanting with the perspective of the floor.

spots.title: A spare blade
spots.text: At the very bottom edge, cut off by the frame, another tool waits. The cropping feels accidental, like a snapshot.

lesson.text: After this picture, Caillebotte became the group's quiet engine. He paid for exhibitions, rented the rooms, and bought his friends' canvases when no one else would, at times covering Monet's rent. For a century he was remembered more as a patron than as a painter.

When he died in 1894 he left his collection, nearly seventy Impressionist works, to the French State. Officials hesitated for years and accepted only about forty. The Floor Scrapers arrived separately, offered by his family that same year.
Caillebotte gave city laborers the scale, the anatomy and the seriousness that painting had reserved for heroes, and he did it without telling you what to think of them.

So, back to the first question. If paintings of people at work no longer surprise you, this floor is one reason. And in a nice twist, the room being prepared by these three men was meant to become the studio where pictures like this would be made.

quiz.question: What do the dark stripes on the floor show?
options: Old varnish that has not been scraped yet
quiz.explanation: Pale areas are bare scraped wood; dark bands are still varnished.

quiz.question: How did the Salon jury react in 1875?
options: It gave it a gold medal
It bought it for the State
quiz.explanation: The subject was judged vulgar and the picture was refused.

quiz.question: What have the workers set down on the right?
options: A bottle of wine and a glass
quiz.explanation: A bottle and a filled glass stand on the hearth.

quiz.question: From where does the viewer seem to look at the scene?
quiz.explanation: The high viewpoint makes the floor fill most of the canvas.

quiz.question: Where did Caillebotte finally exhibit the picture in 1876?
quiz.explanation: He showed it with Monet, Renoir, Degas and Pissarro.

quiz.question: What else was Caillebotte for the Impressionists, besides a fellow painter?
options: A patron who bought their work and funded shows
quiz.explanation: He paid for exhibitions and bought his friends' paintings.

facts.text: About three quarters of the painting is taken up by the floor.
facts.explanation: The wall only begins near the top of the canvas.

facts.text: Caillebotte painted the scene to earn money he badly needed.
facts.explanation: He had inherited a fortune and did not need to sell.

facts.text: The French State gladly accepted every work in Caillebotte's bequest.
facts.explanation: Officials hesitated and accepted only about forty of nearly seventy.
